**Verdict:** He'd tell you not to start a startup yet. He'd also tell you to keep building the side project, and if it takes off on its own, it may be reasonable to run with it. The real question is whether the project is pulling you along, not whether you're 20.

**Based on:** he said it (confidence: high). He spoke to almost exactly your situation at Stanford in 2014, and he came back to it in an August 2026 essay.

**Why he'd say it**
- **The default is no.** "Do not start a startup in college." He says "20 is not the optimal time to do it," because "if you start a startup you're not a student anymore." ([2014 Stanford talk @ 18:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1136s)) In 2026 he still holds that "running a startup is incompatible with being a full time student." ([prepare.html](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html))
- **Waiting costs you nothing.** "You're not sacrificing anything if you forego starting a startup at 20, cuz you'll be more likely to succeed if you wait." He thinks your early twenties are for diving into projects "that seem like they have no payoff." Success takes that freedom away. His example is Zuckerberg: "Facebook is running him as much as he is running Facebook." (2014 @ 21:12, 20:40)
- **The exception is your case.** If a side project takes off, "you face the choice of either running with it or not, and maybe it's reasonable to run with it." ([2014 @ 21:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1272s))
- **He thinks side projects are where startups come from.** "None of these companies were even supposed to be companies at first, they were all just side projects." His test for when one is turning into a company: "You will know that it's becoming a real startup when it takes over an alarming percentage of your life." ([2014 @ 43:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=2595s))
- **In 2026 he leans further toward the exception.** He wants universities to give students free time precisely because "a significant number of those side projects would be incipient startups." He points out that Microsoft and Meta "both got started during reading period at Harvard." When one takes off, he says students must either abandon it "or drop out." ([prepare.html](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html))
- **How he'd want you to spend college:** "just learn." Study CS ("Definitely," even with AI writing code), learn powerful ideas, and build things with people you respect. (2014 @ 30:49; prepare.html)

**What he's done:** He used to tell would-be founders to work at a company for a few years first. By 2014 he called that wrong: "the best way to learn how to start a startup is to try and start it" ([2014 @ 33:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=2016s)). So "wait" means "don't force it while you're a student." It doesn't mean "get a job first."

**What would change his answer:** traction. If real users are adopting the project and it's eating your time whether you like it or not, he'd say running with it may be reasonable. That could mean taking time off or dropping out, since in his view you can't do both well. If you're just excited and want to "be a founder," he'd say keep building, keep learning, and let the project show you whether it's a company. His 2023 essay on superlinear returns adds that the young are the people who "can afford to risk trying it to find out" ([superlinear.html](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)). That supports trying when the moment comes, not starting one for its own sake.

**Caveat:** The 2014 advice was aimed at students. The 2026 essay is aimed at universities and never says outright whether a student should start one. The vault reads this as a shift in emphasis, not a reversal.

**Verdict:** Yes. Paul Graham thinks you should go to Silicon Valley, at least for a while. He doesn't say you have to stay. He gave this advice in a talk in Stockholm (April 2026): *"Should I go there? And the answer is the same now as it always is. Yes, you should. You can go there for a bit and then come back, but you should at least go."* ([talk @ 0:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=36s))

**Based on:** said it. He was answering a Stockholm audience, so this is your situation exactly.

**Why he says it**
- **Peers.** Every field has one center, and moving to it pays off whether or not you cross a border: *"You get the best peers. And in fact, the talent pool expands in two dimensions. The people are better, and there's also a lot more of them."* ([@ 1:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=69s))
- **Chance meetings.** *"if you're working on something ambitious, there's nothing in the world that's better than serendipitous meetings with people who are working on the same stuff."* ([@ 3:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=200s))
- **Investors.** Valley investors decide faster because competition means a good deal won't wait. Investors at home also treat you better once you've left: *"Investors outside Silicon Valley implicitly assume that any local startup is second rate. It's not a uniquely Swedish problem."* and *"if you leave for Silicon Valley, you make this rule operate in reverse."* ([@ 6:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=399s))
- **What it does to you,** which he calls the biggest effect: *"When you're a big fish in a small pond, you don't even know how big a fish you are."* ([@ 8:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=532s)) Once you see the big fish up close, the goal *"no longer seems an impossible goal, just a hard one."* ([@ 10:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=634s))
- **A culture of helping.** *"In Silicon Valley, people help you for no reason."* ([@ 12:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=735s))

**About Stockholm specifically:** Going and then coming back is also his plan for making Stockholm a hub. Founders who return bring better startups, Valley money and Valley culture: *"as long as you do actually come back, that's one of the best things you can do to help Sweden to help Stockholm thrive as a startup hub."* ([@ 16:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=970s)) He says the best way to go for a while is to do YC, and he admits that this sounds like he's *"talking my own book"* ([@ 17:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1036s)).

**The cost of going home:** He says YC startups that return home after the batch *"are only about half as likely to become unicorns."* ([@ 18:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1137s)) He then discounts that number himself. Part of it is selection bias: the founders who stay may simply be more confident and determined. Part of it reflects higher Bay Area valuations rather than better performance.

**What would change his answer:** Not much about the advice itself. He does allow for a personal trade-off: *"Money isn't everything. Once you have kids, you'll find you care more about them than your company."* ([@ 19:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1170s)) If family ties keep you in Stockholm, he would accept that choice. He would still describe it as a trade against your odds of success, not as a free choice.

Keep in mind that he founded YC and profits from founders who come to it, and he says so. On the same topic, Sam Altman (July 2026, also in the vault) agrees that moving was the best way to find co-founders. He says it's probably still good advice but that he's less sure of it now.

I've read Seibel's thinking page and the vault's fundraising pages; writing the answer now.

**Verdict:** Seibel would tell you to stop. Months of pitching, deck polishing and follow-up meetings is the trap he fell into at Justin.tv. Put that time into making the company one investors chase, then raise from that position.

**Based on:** said it (October 2026 Seibel/Caldwell episode on leverage, plus his 2019 MVP talk)

**Why he'd say it**

- **He has lived this.** He spent about eight months trying to raise for Justin.tv. With two months of runway left, the team gave up on fundraising and worked on making the company profitable. He says they got more done in those two months than in all the months of pitching:
  > "we got to figure out how to make this thing profitable or we're going to die." ([yt-7TU636F_yVQ @ 6:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=404s))
  > "if you just think about how much time is wasted, it's like a it's like a drag on the industry." (same @ 6:44)

- **Polishing the deck plays against the odds.** Investors told him they chase 80–90% of their deals; only 10–20% come in through the front door. Pitching harder puts you in the small group.
  > "if you can invest that time in making your company something that investors will chase after versus decksmithing, you're you're playing into the odds versus playing out of the odds." ([yt-7TU636F_yVQ @ 10:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=603s))

- **A deck barely matters when the company is working.** When Socialcam was the number two app in the App Store, the pitch hardly mattered:
  > "one of our pitch decks kind of just was like here's some questions you can ask us." ([yt-7TU636F_yVQ @ 9:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=570s))

- **The deck is worth less than anything a customer can use.**
  > "spending all that time on a pitch deck is not as valuable as spending your time building anything that you can give to a customer." ([yt-1hHMwLxN6EM @ 11:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=671s))

- **Follow-up meetings that go nowhere are usually the investor keeping an option open.** In the same episode, the hosts describe VCs who invest mostly on traction. Stringing you along costs them little and keeps them in if you take off. Your time is what pays for it. This part comes up in back-and-forth without a clear speaker, so it's the episode's view rather than a quote from Seibel.

- **Leverage comes from the work, not from pitch tactics.** When founders ask him how to raise a good round or what goes in a deck, he and Caldwell answer by asking how much leverage they have. Leverage means being able to walk away, and you build it beforehand through growth and a full pipeline. The "ninja tricks" at the end don't create it. He makes the same point about sales: "if you're a customer, you don't like to feel that the company you're considering needs you more than you need them." ([@ 13:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=836s)) Investors work the same way.

**What he'd have you do instead:** Treat fundraising as finished for now. Cut costs and look for a path to default-alive, as he did at Justin.tv. Then spend the hours on customers: launch, sell, grow. When the numbers start pulling investors in, raise quickly.

**What would change his answer:** If you already have strong traction and investors are reaching out to you, your problem isn't fundraising strategy and a short, focused raise makes sense. Also, he doesn't treat investor rejection as a verdict on the idea. He points out that Coinbase struggled to raise at Demo Day, and he'd say the same if every no feels like a judgment ([yt-Jcuqq48CNj8 @ 12:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=723s)).

**Caveat from the vault:** The fundraising episode is co-hosted by Dalton Caldwell, whose Series A fund, Standard Capital, sponsors the show. "Investors waste founders' time; good ones don't" is partly a pitch for his fund. The Justin.tv story is Seibel's own experience, though, and that part doesn't depend on the sponsorship.

**Verdict:** Seibel would tell you to fire the lawyers and settle this yourselves within a week. Your cofounder hands back most of his stock, vested or not, and keeps around 1–2% (maybe under 1%) since he's leaving inside the first year. You pay him reasonable severance and you both sign clean paperwork.

His reasoning: before product-market fit the stock is worth nothing, so a legal fight is a fight over ego. Lawyers profit from your anger, and almost all of the company's value still has to be built by whoever stays.

**Based on:** said it. He addressed this exact situation in a July 2026 Dalton + Michael episode, [*Do You Need a Co-Founder for Your Startup?*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U)

**Why he'd say it**
- **Lawyers make no sense here:** "in a situation where you're having a co-founder breakup and the stock is worth nothing, paying lawyers a bunch of money makes no sense." ([@ 11:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=696s)) And: "a lawyer can suck up infinite amount of your ... anger and monetize it." ([@ 12:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=727s))
- **Vested stock doesn't change it:** "even if you vested, like get down to under 5% of the company, if it's within the first year, under 2%." ([@ 18:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1119s)) Later in the episode: "After a number of years, 5% typical. Under a year, 1%, 2%, sometimes less than 1%." ([@ 21:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1282s))
- **The equity belongs with the people who stay:** "the vast majority of the value this company could create hasn't been created yet." He also says the company needs "as much equity as possible to motivate the people who are there" ([@ 14:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=887s)). His argument for why the leaver should accept this: "you get to hedge. The founder staying doesn't." ([@ 15:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=921s))
- **His whole process:** "Do reasonable severance, sign clean paperwork and and peace out". He adds that "you could do that whole thing in a week and spend like $2,000." ([@ 18:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1119s))
- **Stop wasting time:** "when you really know the probability of success is zero, most important thing is to stop wasting time." ([@ 9:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=566s))
- **If you bring in someone to help:** "If you're using someone to mediate this, don't make them the judge." ([@ 19:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1186s)) Dalton Caldwell, his co-host, makes the same point: "the facts don't matter. I'm not the judge and jury." The goal is a plan for going forward, not a ruling on who was right.
- **If you're the one staying:** Be generous and act as the responsible party. "it is so cheap to be nice", and "everyone in your company is looking at you right now." ([@ 17:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1053s)) He also takes the blame off your cofounder: "If you made a list of all the things we screwed up in our company, it would be way longer than the things you're pissed at your co-founder about." ([@ 21:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=1314s))

**What he's done:** When a cofounder leaves, Seibel says he often talks to the departing founder first and makes the case for leaving the equity with the team that stays. YC has written breakup standards so both founders get the same advice.

**What would change his answer:**
- **Misconduct:** "if your co-founder is breaking the law, doing something unethical, killing people, none of this applies." (@ 21:54)
- **Real value in the company:** All of this assumes the company is before product-market fit and the stock is close to worthless. If it has real traction or value, his "the stock is worth nothing" premise no longer holds.

**Caveats:**
- **Attribution:** The vault rates most of these quotes as medium confidence. They come from auto-captions where some lines are assigned to Seibel because they continue his turn. The 21:22 percentages, the 21:54 lines and "Don't get fooled by service providers" are high confidence.
- **Not legal advice:** You still need a lawyer to draft the final paperwork. Seibel's point is that it should be a cheap, quick, agreed document, not letters going back and forth.
- **Your vesting (my note, not Seibel's):** Standard four-year vesting has a one-year cliff, so at 9 months nothing would normally be vested. If he really has vested a chunk, check your stock agreements for the actual terms before you negotiate.

That was Sam Altman, not Garry Tan. His one reason is network effects. A bigger network means more chances to meet your future co-founders, so the network's lead over everyone else keeps growing.

**Based on:** said it. The source is Altman's conversation with Tan at YC's July 2026 event ([video @ 16:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1016s)).

**What he said.** Altman spoke while Tan was interviewing him. He made the point himself because, as YC's current head, Tan couldn't credibly make it:

> "I also think that I I can say this, Gary probably can't. I I I think the premium on doing YC is bigger now than it's like ever been before. Uh, the distance between like YC and second place is has expanded. And this is a reminder of the power of network effects." (@ 16:56–17:28)

**Why, in his words:**
- **It's a network-effects business.** He sees the widening gap as "a reminder of the power of network effects." The more good founders YC gathers, the more valuable joining it becomes, so the leader pulls further ahead.
- **The network is where co-founders come from.** He brings it up while answering how to find co-founders. He says that five or ten years earlier, the main thing limiting how many good startups YC could fund was "figuring out how to solve the co-founder matching problem" (@ 16:25). He met the people he started OpenAI with "many many years in some cases before uh starting OpenAI" (@ 17:28).
- **It takes a long time to pay off.** "the sooner you can put yourself just in a flow where you're going to meet the people that will be your eventual co-founders … the better. It takes a long time to compound." (@ 17:28–18:02)
- **YC is the new Bay Area.** The old answer was to move to the Bay Area, where "magic happened. You got a lot of like lucky chances and collisions." He still thinks that's "probably good advice, although I feel like I have less of an intuition for it now" (@ 16:56). In context, YC now plays that role.

**Who backs it up:**
- Tan's part of the conversation is about the same network, not about any premium: "this is the kind of like loose network and the spirit of helping each other and this like very long-term outlook has been an awesome thing" (@ 23:35).
- Paul Graham makes the same point in an essay: "YC itself is an instance of network effects in something you wouldn't expect to have them. We didn't intend it to be, but we realized very quickly that that was what we'd stumbled upon." ([[web-19ac0b6d18d2]])

**Caveats:**
- Altman is YC's former president and said this at a YC event. His "Gary probably can't" admits the conflict of interest.
- He gives no numbers or evidence for the "second place" gap. It's his read of the network, not a measurement.

The vault's leaf on this is `vaults/yc/wiki/hiring/cofounders/finding-cofounders-and-your-people.md`. It credits the claim to Altman correctly.

**The vault says the opposite.** Jessica Livingston never says early YC backed the most aggressive, ruthless founders. In the one place she uses those words, she's describing *investors*, and she sets herself against them. On founders, her filter was earnestness, and she turned away people she thought were conceited.

**Based on:** she said it (one 2018 talk, with support from a 2024 interview).

**Where "aggressive" and "ruthless" come from**
In her 2018 Female Founders talk ("9 Things She Learned From Founding YC"), she uses the words to describe the VC culture YC was reacting against:
- "I was soft and sensitive at a time when investors tended to be hardened and aggressive and I'll throw in ruthless" ([yt-8d-cApFHjeY @ 17:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1064s))
- Right after that, she says she "cared about how founders were feeling if they were overwhelmed if they were eating properly," counselled them on strained relationships and helped with co-founder breakups (@ 17:44–18:18).

**What she actually screened for**
- "did they seem earnest did they seem determined were they flexible minded and most importantly what was the relationship between the co-founders like" ([@ 14:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=891s))
- "from the beginning I was very careful about only funding earnest people" (@ 14:51)
- "if I could tell someone was a conceited we did not fund them" and "early on I was pretty rigid about this and I think that's the basis of the culture of our alumni community" (@ 15:27)
- In 2024 she said: "Earnest and not pretentious that's in YC's DNA" ([yt-6u4JVz7iQTY @ 45:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=2734s))

**What's true in the premise**
She did want tough founders, just not ruthless ones:
- "Determined" is one of her four tests, and in 2024 she said of the founders she'd known that "they're all very determined" (@ 51:43).
- She values boldness: "you do need a certain amount of boldness to work on ideas that most people would consider stupid and to keep going when you're ridiculed or ignored" (2018 @ 25:45).
- Paul Graham (her husband and YC co-founder) says "formidable" comes from his and Livingston's private language. He defines it as "someone who gets what they want in any situation" ([yt-5bxp78i96S8 @ 9:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=597s)). That's about getting results, not about how you treat people. It's also his definition, not hers.

**Why she rejected the ruthless type**
- **Culture compounds.** She says her rigid early screen for earnest, unconceited founders is "the basis of the culture of our alumni community." YC depends on alumni helping new founders: "Our Best Contacts were our alumni" (2024 @ 28:12).
- **Co-founder relationships decide outcomes.** She calls that relationship the "most important" thing she judged. She also advises picking "a co-founder with complementary skills but the same moral compass as you" (2018 @ 23:59).
- **YC was meant to be kinder than VCs.** She says she doesn't "get why investors squeeze founders over small outcomes" (2018 @ 20:36). Having no LPs let YC "be benevolent to failing startups" (@ 19:26).

**What would change this:** a source where she says she prefers aggressive or ruthless founders. The vault has only two Livingston talks (2018 and 2024), and neither says that. She admits YC has "since funded some conceited" founders, but she presents that as a slip from her standard, not a policy.

**Caveat:** both sources come from YC (a YC conference talk and a YC-produced podcast), so this is how she presents YC in public, not an outside account.
